summary: Sets out the issues involved in joining the IP integrated services environment to ATM so that applications get a seamless interface with real-time support. It is an informational statement of the problem.

eli5.summary: Two kinds of networks reserve space differently. This memo lists what must be sorted out so they can work together.

questions: how do ip integrated services work with atm
what are the issues of ip over atm real-time
how do ip and atm integrate for real-time services
what are the differences between rsvp and atm signalling
what routing issues arise with ip over atm
subtitle: Bridging two different approaches to reserving network resources for real-time traffic.

tldr.problem: The IETF was developing IP's integrated services environment for real-time traffic (voice and video) while the ATM Forum was developing ATM networks with similar capabilities. When IP runs over ATM, the two different service models must work together, but they are fundamentally different in how they manage resources.
tldr.mechanism: This memo analyzes the key technical issues that arise when mapping IP's dynamic, receiver-initiated reservation model onto ATM's static, sender-initiated, connection-oriented service model, covering traffic characterization, QoS specification, routing, and security.
tldr.outcome: It identifies five major problem areas (service models, reservation styles, routing, multicast, and security) and lists areas for future standards work, but does not solve the problems.

today: RFC 1821 is an Informational memo that remains a valuable analysis of the IP-ATM integration challenge. The questions it raises were addressed over the following decade through standards work on Integrated Services, MPLS, and subsequent ATM enhancements.

sections.title: The Challenge of IP Over ATM
sections.content:
The IETF's Integrated Services initiative and the ATM Forum's service model both promise to carry real-time applications like video teleconferencing over networks. However, they solve the problem in very different ways. The IP approach uses dynamic resource reservations that can change at any time, initiated by the receiver. ATM uses static connections set up by the sender that cannot change without tearing down and recreating the connection.

When IP datagrams are carried as cells inside an ATM network, routers at the edge of the ATM cloud must translate between the two models. This memo explores what issues arise in doing so and what work is needed to create a seamless real-time service across both types of networks.
sections.eli5: IP and ATM both promise to deliver video calls reliably, but they use completely different machinery. Getting them to work together requires solving many hard problems.

sections.title: Service Models and Their Differences
sections.content:
A real-time service model needs two things: a way to describe the traffic (the Tspec, or traffic specification, often a token bucket) and a way to describe the desired quality of service (the Rspec, or QoS specification). The IP model proposes three service classes: guaranteed (with a mathematically proven delay bound), predictive delay (probabilistic), and controlled delay. ATM defines five classes: CBR (constant bit rate, like a leased line), VBR-real-time (variable bit rate with tight delay), VBR-non-real-time, UBR (unspecified bit rate, best-effort), and ABR (available bit rate with feedback control).

These classes do not directly map to each other. An IP guaranteed flow might be transported using ATM CBR, but that would be inefficient and expensive. A better approach might use ATM VBR, but it is unclear how to preserve the IP service guarantees when traffic becomes burstier in transit through the network. Loss rates also pose a problem: cell loss in ATM can cause entire IP packets to drop, multiplying the effective loss rate.
sections.eli5: IP offers three kinds of service quality. ATM offers five. They are not the same, and figuring out how to translate between them is hard.

sections.title: Resource Reservation Protocols
sections.content:
IP's RSVP protocol is receiver-initiated, uses soft state (reservations time out and must be refreshed), and allows dynamic changes to QoS. ATM's signalling protocol (Q.2931) is sender-initiated, uses hard state (explicit deletion required), and fixes QoS at connection setup. A second IP protocol, ST-II, is more like ATM: sender-initiated and hard state, but still allows dynamic QoS changes.

Mapping RSVP to ATM requires routers to manage ATM connections that come and go as RSVP reservations arrive and expire. If a RSVP soft-state reservation times out, the router must tear down the ATM virtual circuit, but if it does this too aggressively, the next reservation for the same destination may fail because resources are no longer allocated. Different service classes have different cost trade-offs for keeping connections open. ST-II is easier to map to ATM but still faces issues when multiple flows arrive for the same destination but the existing ATM connection cannot be modified to accommodate higher QoS.
sections.eli5: IP lets receivers say "I want service" and change their mind later. ATM requires the sender to commit upfront and set it in stone. Teaching them to work together requires careful negotiation of who decides and when.

sections.title: Routing and Path Selection
sections.content:
ATM routers choose a path once at connection setup and stick with it, consulting only a connection identifier on each cell. IP routers consult the destination address on every packet, allowing routes to change dynamically. When QoS is involved, route changes are problematic: a new route might have different available bandwidth and delay characteristics, violating the QoS contract.

This is especially acute for multicast and QoS routing. No current multicast protocols communicate QoS requirements at tree setup time, leaving RSVP to establish QoS after the tree is built, potentially requiring expensive recomputation. QoS routing itself is expensive (computing routes for every possible combination of QoS and destination), but necessary for real-time services. The ATM Forum's PNNI protocol includes QoS information in routing advertisements, which could help, but IP routing protocols do not currently support this.
sections.eli5: ATM picks a path once and never changes it. IP can reroute each packet. When quality matters, neither approach is ideal.

sections.title: Guarding Against Abuse
sections.content:
When network resources are reserved, a malicious user could deny service to others by reserving resources without authorization. The IP and ATM communities have different security architectures, creating a potential weak point in an integrated network. An attacker might access the network via the IP side to request ATM resources without proper credentials, or vice versa.

The memo recommends that trusted edge devices be required to request QoS resources on behalf of untrusted hosts as a near-term solution. The IETF is developing IP security mechanisms (authentication headers and key management), and these should be coordinated with ATM security work to ensure compatibility.
sections.eli5: If someone can book network resources for free, they might book them all and break the network for everyone else. IP and ATM need to agree on how to check IDs.

sections.title: Areas for Future Work
sections.content: The memo identifies five major areas where standards development is needed. First, define specific mappings from IP Tspecs and Rspecs to ATM service classes and parameters, and validate that ATM can reliably provide the promised QoS. Second, determine how RSVP and ST-II signalling map onto ATM connection establishment. Third, develop better QoS routing protocols that can select paths based on QoS constraints, not just hop count. Fourth, extend ATM to support dynamic QoS modification (changing a connection's service after setup) and more flexible multicast (allowing different QoS to different receivers, and multipoint-to-multipoint connections). Fifth, consider enhancements to the IP service model, such as a sender-initiated mode for RSVP, to better align with ATM's capabilities.
sections.eli5: There are five big things nobody knows how to do yet. Once we build and operate integrated networks, we will learn what works and refine the standards.
